eyebrow: Problem 1: self-orthogonality of row 2 and row 3 of H
code:
Row 2 = [0,1,1,0,0,1,1]
Row 3 = [1,0,1,0,1,0,1]

Entrywise product: [0,0,1,0,0,0,1]
Sum mod 2: 0+0+1+0+0+0+1 = 2 = 0 (mod 2)

-> rows overlap in exactly 2 positions (3 and 7) -> self-orthogonal, confirmed
caption: Verified computationally alongside every other row pair, including each row with itself.

eyebrow: Problem 2: syndromes from column lookup on H
code:
H columns:  col3=[0,1,1]  col5=[1,0,1]  col7=[1,1,1]

X error on qubit 3  -> Z-type syndrome (0,1,1)
Z error on qubit 5  -> X-type syndrome (1,0,1)
X error on qubit 7  -> Z-type syndrome (1,1,1)  (every row has a 1)
caption: Read the column for that qubit number — those are exactly the stabilizers that flip. No quantum state simulation needed.

steps.label: Column lookup is a purely classical operation on H
steps.sub: Inherited directly from the classical Hamming(7,4) code's structure

steps.label: No need to track quantum amplitudes at all
steps.sub: Because the stabilizers are built directly from a classical parity-check matrix

steps.label: This is the practical payoff of the CSS construction
steps.sub: Syndrome computation reduces to linear algebra over H

steps.label: This same shortcut scales to much larger codes
steps.sub: Including the surface code's lattice, coming up in Chapter 5
